answer: History, not a forecast. Nursing care facility prices (producer price index, Dec 1994 to Mar 2026) rose 3.52% a year over the whole period; over the 136 overlapping 20-year stretches they rose between 2.78% and 3.61% a year (median 3.1%). A daily benefit that started out covering the full daily price would, 20 years later, cover a median 54.3% with no inflation option, 98.1% with 3% compound (range 88.9% to 104.4%; full coverage in 44.1% of stretches) and 144.1% with 5% compound (never below 130.6%). In this price record the 3% option came close to keeping pace and the 5% option ran well ahead of prices in every stretch.
guess: Insurance marketing and many articles say care costs rise about 5% a year, faster than general inflation, so buyers would guess a 3% option falls far behind and only the 5% option keeps up.
changesDecision: The 5% option costs noticeably more in premium. If the buyer's reason for paying for it is 'care prices rise 5% a year', this price record does not show that for nursing care facilities since 1994: 3% compounding never fell more than about 11% short of prices over any 20-year stretch, while 5% compounding outran them by a wide margin. That may change how a buyer weighs the premium difference (or what daily benefit to start with), although local prices, private-pay rates and future inflation can differ. The episode reports the history; it does not recommend an option.

assumptions: The policy's daily benefit starts equal to the daily price of care at the start of the window and grows by r compounded annually (r = 0, 3% or 5%) for 20 years.

Nursing care prices are measured by the national producer price index for nursing care facilities (what facilities receive per unit of service, all payers), which is a stand-in for the private-pay daily rate a policyholder faces.
Overlapping monthly start dates; the index begins in Dec 1994, so only starts from Dec 1994 to Mar 2006 have a full 20 years.
Data pinned at Mar 2026 because the most recent PPI months are preliminary and revised for four months.
Premium differences between the options and premium increases on in-force policies are not modeled.
limits: History, not a forecast. The price record covers only about 31 years, so the 136 windows overlap heavily (roughly one and a half independent 20-year periods). The producer price index blends Medicare, Medicaid and private payers and is national; private-pay prices in a given city, assisted living and home care can grow faster or slower. Says nothing about premiums or claim likelihood.
